system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Ms. ___ was admitted for worsening wheezing, cough, and shortness of breath after a prolonged course at rehab, where she had been treated for suspected pneumonia without improvement. Evaluation revealed an acute exacerbation of COPD and acute on chronic systolic heart failure, supported by elevated BNP and clinical signs of fluid overload. She was treated with a short course of high-dose prednisone, nebulized albuterol and ipratropium, and a brief increase in lasix dose, which was stopped when renal function and sodium began to decline. A CT scan of the neck and chest showed no evidence of tracheal cancer recurrence but noted new left upper lobe consolidation, which was deemed non-infectious given her clinical improvement. She remained in normal sinus rhythm on amiodarone and metoprolol. Discharge planning included a structured steroid taper, resumption of lasix only if weight exceeded 87kg, and follow-up with pulmonology, oncology in six months, and vascular surgery for planned toe amputations due to gangrene. She was discharged to extended care in stable condition.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Chronic obstructive asthma with (acute) exacerbation
Atherosclerosis of native arteries of the extremities with gangrene
Atrial fibrillation
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of trachea
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of breast
Chronic kidney disease, unspecified
Congestive heart failure, unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  Shortness of breath, hypoxia.

FINDINGS:  A single portable semi-erect chest radiograph was obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT ___.  

Radiographs ___ through ___.

FINDINGS:  Right lower lobe and retrocardiac opacities have significantly
worsened since ___ and now obscure the bilateral diaphragmatic
contours.  Post-surgical volume loss and minor fissure thickening are more
pronounced.  Cardiomegaly is similar.  A right shoulder prosthesis is similar.

IMPRESSION:  Significant worsening of multifocal opacities representing some
combination of atelectasis, pulmonary edema and consolidation.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with flash pulmonary edema and poor intravenous
access.  Please advance midline to central location.

PHYSICIANS:  Dr. ___ (resident) and Dr. ___ (fellow)
performed the procedure.  Dr. ___ (attending) was present for and
supervised the critical steps of the procedure.

PROCEDURE IN DETAIL:  The procedure was explained to the patient.  A
preprocedure timeout was performed.  The entry site containing the existing
PICC was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  Under fluoroscopy,
the position of the existing catheter was confirmed to be in the left axillary
vein. The skin and subcutaneous tissues were anesthetized with 2% lidocaine at
the entry site.  A guidewire was advanced through the existing catheter with
the tip in the left axillary vein.  The guidewire could not be advanced past
the axillary vein, likely due to stenosis in the subclavian vein.  The patient
confirmed that she has had a prior Port-A-Cath on the left as seen on prior
chest radiographs. After phone discussion with the ordering physician, it was
confirmed that a midline would be adequate.  The existing catheter was removed
and a peel-away sheath was placed over the guidewire.  A double-lumen Power
PICC measuring 22 cm in length was placed through the peel-away sheath with
its tip positioned in the axillary vein under fluoroscopic guidance.  Position
of the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest.  The
peel-away sheath and guidewire were removed.  The catheter was secured to the
skin, flushed and a sterile dressing applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate post-procedure
complications.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Uncomplicated fluoroscopically guided double-lumen midline placement via
the left brachial approach (per documentation of prior catheter placement). 
Final internal length is 22 cm with the tip positioned in the left axillary
vein.  The line is ready to use.
2.  Probable left subclavian vein stenosis due to prior left Port-A-Cath.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST X-RAY

INDICATION:  Patient with CHF, asthma, CKD, tracheobronchomalacia, history
tracheal cancer, recently in ICU for pulmonary edema, followup.

COMPARISON:  Chest x-ray from ___ to ___.  Chest CT of ___.

FINDINGS:

Bilateral lung opacities have completely resolved.  Right upper lobe lobectomy
with radiation changes and juxtaphrenic peak sign are unchanged.  Mediastinal
and cardiac contours are stable.  Bilateral humeral prostheses.  Left-sided
PICC line ends in axillary region.

CONCLUSION:

1.  Bilateral lung opacities have completely resolved since ___.

2.  Left-sided PICC line ends in axillary region.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You’re in the ICU right now because you were having a lot of trouble breathing. You’re on a CPAP machine, which is helping you breathe easier. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better with this mask, but it’s uncomfortable. I couldn’t catch my breath at the home. I think I missed some of my pills… there are so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We saw that you were overloaded with fluid, especially in your lungs. That’s why you were short of breath. We gave you a strong diuretic, lasix, and you’ve already passed about half a liter. That’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But I didn’t have a fever or cough this time. Is it another infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think it’s an infection. Your chest X-ray shows fluid buildup, not pneumonia. You also had very high blood pressure when you arrived—over 200. That likely pushed fluid into your lungs. We’ve started medications to bring that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did eat a few salty meals last week… I know I shouldn’t. But with all my meds, I just get overwhelmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay—we’re going to help simplify your medications. We know it’s a lot. For now, we’re focusing on getting your breathing and blood pressure under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your sodium is low—129. That’s common when you retain fluid. We’ll watch it closely. Also, your white blood cell count is high, so we gave one dose of antibiotics just in case, but we’re stopping them now since there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my kidneys? I’ve had trouble before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your kidney function is stable—creatinine is 1.6, which is elevated but not worsening. We’re being careful with fluids and meds to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We moved your IV to your arm today because the one in your groin was temporary. The new line is safer and more comfortable. You’re doing well—we’re planning to move you to the regular floor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I stop using the CPAP soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wean it off slowly. Your breathing is improving, but we want to make sure the fluid doesn’t come back. Your last chest X-ray still shows some congestion, but it’s getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your breathing is much better. You’re off CPAP now and on regular oxygen. Your chest X-ray from yesterday shows the fluid in your lungs is clearing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my heart? I’ve had AFib before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve stayed in normal rhythm this whole time. We’re keeping you on amiodarone and adding carvedilol, which helps your heart and blood pressure. We switched from metoprolol to make your med schedule easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma? I still feel a little tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have underlying asthma and some tracheal narrowing from past treatments. We’re continuing your albuterol nebs and adding a new inhaler—Advair—to help control inflammation and keep your airways open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Advair? I’ve heard of that. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. It combines a steroid and a long-acting bronchodilator. We’re also keeping you on prednisone for now, but we’ll taper it down to avoid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We simplified your medications. You’re now on lisinopril for blood pressure and heart protection, carvedilol twice a day instead of four times, and a daily lasix to prevent fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fewer pills. I like that. But I’m still on prednisone? I’ve been on steroids before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of your asthma and recent flare-up. But we’ll taper it over the next few weeks. Long-term use can cause problems, so your primary doctor will help manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the fluid is completely gone. That’s excellent progress. Your breathing should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What about my toes? They’ve been black for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have dry gangrene from poor circulation. We’ll need to follow up with vascular surgery. They’ll likely recommend amputation to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was afraid of that. It doesn’t hurt, but I know it’s serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we’re staying ahead of it. No signs of infection now. We’ll coordinate that follow-up before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood again—your sodium is improving, and kidney function is stable. We’ll keep watching potassium now that you’re on lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anemia? I’ve always been low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 27%, which is low. Iron and ferritin are high, so it’s not a typical deficiency. Your primary doctor should look into that further as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’ll go home with services—someone will help you with daily tasks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’s great. But I’m nervous about managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve made your med list much simpler. You’ll take carvedilol twice a day, lisinopril, lasix, Advair, albuterol as needed, and a few others. We’ll send a list to your daughter and your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve been on Percocet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue oxycodone-acetaminophen as needed. We noted a suggestion to switch to OxyContin, but that’s something your doctor can consider later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to shellfish and aspirin. Are all my meds safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. We’re avoiding anything with shellfish derivatives. And because of your aspirin allergy, you’re on clopidogrel for blood thinning instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also want to talk about your advance care plan. You’re listed as full code. Would you like to discuss that with your daughter before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I’d like her to be part of that conversation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with your daughter. She’ll be your main contact. We’ve scheduled follow-ups with your primary doctor, pulmonology, and vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And the prednisone—I’ll need to taper it slowly, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re sending you home on 20 mg daily. Your doctor will help you reduce it over the next few weeks to avoid withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cholesterol? I’m not on a statin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It’s not started here, but we’ve recommended your primary doctor consider it. We’ll include that in your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re breathing well, your labs are stable, and your heart is strong. We’re discharging you home with visiting nurse services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so grateful. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember: take your meds as listed, watch your salt, weigh yourself daily, and call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or have trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep my follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll make sure your daughter gets a copy of everything. Take care, Ms. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: Ms. ___ was admitted for acute respiratory failure and hypertensive emergency leading to pulmonary edema. She presented with severe dyspnea and was initially managed in the MICU with CPAP and IV furosemide, resulting in significant improvement. Her condition was complicated by medication noncompliance and a high pill burden, which contributed to fluid overload. Antibiotics were briefly administered due to leukocytosis but discontinued as infection was ruled out. She transitioned to the medicine floor, where her heart failure and asthma were managed with optimized medications, including initiation of lisinopril, carvedilol, and fluticasone-salmeterol. Her chest X-ray showed complete resolution of pulmonary opacities. Medication reconciliation simplified her regimen. She remained in sinus rhythm throughout. Discharge planning included a steroid taper, follow-up for gangrene with vascular surgery, and coordination with her primary care provider for ongoing management of anemia, hyperlipidemia, and advance care planning. She was discharged home with services in stable condition.
